title: Is there no balm? (Jeremiah 8:22)
hookLine: "Is there no balm in Gilead?" the prophet weeps for his people's hurt
carry: he stays, and he hurts with them

lines: IS THERE NO BALM IN GILEAD?
cards: "Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there?" To hear the sting in that question, you need to know what Gilead meant.
In Genesis, Joseph's brothers, about to sell him, look up and see a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead, their camels bearing spicery and balm and myrrh, going down to Egypt.
In that story, Gilead is where the balm comes from. So Jeremiah's question is like standing in a pharmacy and asking: is there no medicine here? Of course there is.

teach.b: Listen to the verses just before. "The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved." The season for gathering has come and gone, and nothing was gathered in.

teach.h: FOR THE HURT OF MY PEOPLE AM I HURT.
teach.b: Then Jeremiah's own voice breaks through: "For the hurt of the daughter of my people am I hurt." This is the man who has spent chapter after chapter warning, accusing, calling the people back from broken cisterns.

Here he isn't standing above them. Their wound is his wound. Then the question: "Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there? why then is not the health of the daughter of my people recovered?"

teach.h: THE CURE IS REAL. WHY NO HEALING?
teach.b: The question doesn't doubt that healing exists. The balm is real; the physician is there. What baffles him is the gap between the cure and the patient.
And the verse doesn't answer. Right after it, Jeremiah wishes his head were waters and his eyes a fountain of tears, so he could weep day and night for his people.
Tradition says Jeremiah also wrote the book of Lamentations, and the Talmud records that view.

teach.h: ANGER AND GRIEF IN ONE CHEST.
teach.b: Whether or not you read it that way, here is a prophet whose anger and grief live in the same chest.
There is a particular pain in watching help exist and still not reach: the friend who won't call the doctor, the family that won't talk. Jeremiah doesn't fix it. He stays, and he hurts with them.

how: Jeremiah 8 and 9 are read in synagogue as the haftarah on the morning of Tisha b'Av, the fast day of mourning, when Lamentations is also read aloud.

o: balm, the medicine that came from Gilead
a bitter herb eaten at the Passover meal
the oil used to anoint Israel's kings

games.q: is there no balm? — tap the pairs.
p: for the hurt of my people

s: Jeremiah doubts that any cure exists
the balm is real and the physician is there; he asks why healing hasn't reached his people.
Genesis shows a caravan carrying balm from Gilead
the caravan in Joseph's story came from Gilead bearing spicery, balm and myrrh.
the verse answers its own question
it stays a question, and Jeremiah turns to tears.

games.q: you're a prophet who has warned your people for years, and now they're wounded. what do you do?
o: hurt with them and weep for them.
walk away and let them learn.
games.why: for the hurt of the daughter of my people am I hurt: Jeremiah's anger and grief live side by side.

practice: Let one person come to mind who is in pain right now, in body or in spirit, someone help hasn't reached yet.
Don't try to solve it; just let their hurt sit next to you for a moment, the way Jeremiah let his people's hurt be his own.
Then picture one small act of care that could carry a little balm the last few steps: a message, a meal, a ride to an appointment.

wordCard.voice: Tsori. Hebrew for balm: Jeremiah's cry that the cure is in Gilead, so why are my people not healed? Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: is there no balm in Gilead? tsori is balm, from Jeremiah 8:22.

carryVoice: Your line: he stays, and he hurts with them. Sometimes presence is the balm. Eight hundred days now.
